title: Compliance and Auditability

content.intro: This lesson focuses on compliance and auditability. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Auditability depends on recorded approvals, workflow run history, source-to-artifact traceability, scoped credentials, and reviewable policy changes. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Workflow execution records
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Deployment history
items.text: For deployment history, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Permission reviews
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.title: Secret-management processes
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: Retention and evidence requirements
items.text: For retention and evidence requirements, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
name: Record deployment evidence
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  record:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Write audit summary
        run: |
          {
            echo "## Run evidence"
            echo "- Repository: $GITHUB_REPOSITORY"
            echo "- Commit: $GITHUB_SHA"
            echo "- Run ID: $GITHUB_RUN_ID"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
content_blocks.expected_output: The workflow summary records non-sensitive identifiers that can help correlate a run to source and its run history.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Check that the summary contains only approved metadata and links to the run record.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not place tokens, secrets, customer data, or unrestricted payloads in the audit summary.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to compliance and auditability. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain compliance and auditability, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Standardize workflow behavior across teams without hiding important security boundaries.

content.task: Apply compliance and auditability to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Auditability depends on recorded approvals, workflow run history, source-to-artifact traceability, scoped credentials, and reviewable policy changes.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Auditability depends on recorded approvals, workflow run history, source-to-artifact traceability, scoped credentials, and reviewable policy changes. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Auditability depends on recorded approvals, workflow run history, source-to-artifact traceability, scoped credentials, and reviewable policy changes.
Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
